rejected: Capacitation is the process which occurs when sperm meet female secretions in the female reproductive tract. The cortical reaction is where the surrounding glycoproteins of the ovum bind to sperm in order to select the most fit sperm out of hundreds that have been capacitated. The chemical potential is equal to the standard potential minus the log of the activity of the ion in solution. This gives you the number of electrons you get from 1 mole of the ion when it goes from the standard state to its own standard state. Once you have this you put it into the Nernst equation which gives you the membrane potential. x=61log(Ao/Ac) where x is the potential in volts and Ao and Ac are the standard and activity of the ion respectively. If you know the membrane potential you can find the activity of the ion using the same equation but with the information filled in. The equation doesn't tell you anything about the concentration gradients between the intracellular and extracellular solutions. To work these out you need to use the Stewart-Hamilton equation. This is similar to the Nernst equation except you take the reciprocal instead of the log. So instead of giving you the membrane potential it gives you the concentration difference between the two sides. x=61/CAo where x is the concentration difference in moles and CAo is the membrane potential in vol

correct_option_text: The membrane potential for a particular ion

chosen: The patient is displaying signs of a posterior left hip dislocation. This is because the left leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated. These are all characteristics of a posterior dislocation.  Hip fracture - patient would be unable to bear weightAcetabular labral tear - patient would have localised pain in the groin/sagittal planeAnterior dislocations - legs would be extended, abducted and externally rotatedPosterior dislocations - legs would be flexed, adducted and internally rotated Medial thigh pain is also present in anterior dislocations. Hip dislocations are serious injuries as they can also damage blood vessels and nerves surrounding the area, as well as result in paralysis. Usually the anterior dislocations occur more commonly than posterior dislocations but due to the muscles in the posterior acting as abductors, it is easier to dislocate in a posterior direction due to the lack of tension placed on the ligaments. chosen: Vitamin B9 (folic acid) is essential in the early development of life and a lack of it can cause neural tube defects. Taken from ‘Nutrition in Growth and Development’ lecture by Dr Andrew Shore in Case 7.  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537140/#:~:text=The%20recommended%20daily%20allowance%20(RDA,defects%20in%20the%20developing%20foetus.&text=Folic%20acid%20is%20added%20to,cereals%2C%20and%20enriched%20breads.&text=Women%20who%20are%20pregnant,%2C%20or%20trying%20for%20a%20baby.&text=This%20is%20because%20their%20baby's,of%20the%20neural%20tube%20closes.&text=
rejected: Vitamin B9 (folate/folic acid) is required for DNA synthesis and therefore its addition to foods reduces the risk of neural tube defects. It should be taken for 3 months before conception and for 3 months into the pregnancy. However, it is very difficult to get women to take folate supplements for this length of time so the idea of adding it to foods was developed instead. 80% of neural tube defects occur within the first 6 weeks of pregnancy and often before the woman is aware that she is pregnant. Therefore, the aim is to increase the amount of folate in the diet before conception occurs. Folate deficiency can also cause megaloblastic anaemia. Sources of folate are green vegetables, legumes, citrus fruits and liver. Vitamin B9 becomes vitamin B11 when it has been converted into its coenzyme form - folate is not an intermediate step. Vitamin B9 is water soluble and can be destroyed by heat and light. It cannot be stored in the body so we need a constant supply from our diet. Too much vitamin B9 can mask pernicious anaemia. Vitamin B9 can cross the placenta. Excess amounts can stay in the baby's system after birth and lead to increased risk of leukaemia.
